deep.reconstruction:
Context (end of previous page): the 'basic problem of reduction' is to reduce a system of n real linear forms f_i(x) = sum_k a_ik x_k (i=1..n), i.e. a real n x n matrix a = (a_ik), regarded as a point of R^{n^2}. Two systems are equivalent if one arises from the other by an integral unimodular substitution x -> U x, U in GL_n(Z). Then a -> a U, which is a right action of GL_n(Z) on R^{n^2}.

(1) Statements of the theory, as claims without proof. (a) The reduced domain R in R^{n^2} (a fundamental domain for a -> aU) is bounded by finitely many hyperplanes and is 'nirgends konkav', Minkowski's term for convex. So R is a convex polyhedral region, a cone since the action commutes with scaling. (b) The infinitely many images R U, U in GL_n(Z), accumulate ('verdichten sich') only on the determinant hypersurface A = det(a) = 0. (c) Open question attributed to Minkowski: is the content of the reduced domain finite for A = 1, and what is it? Presumably meant is the volume of {a in R : |det a| <= 1}, or the induced measure on det = 1.

(2) 'Beweisprincip', a Dirichlet/Voronoi-type construction of the fundamental domain. Take an arbitrary point a0 in R^{n^2}. Let a cube W centred at a0 grow continuously, and simultaneously form all its images W U. These are convex, since images of a cube under linear maps are parallelotopes. First one must show that for sufficiently small edge length all the images W U are pairwise disjoint.

(3) Argument for (2). The group GL_n(Z) acting on the n variables x is 'uneigentlich' (improperly discontinuous: e.g. x = 0 is fixed by all U, and orbits accumulate). The holoedrically isomorphic group acting on the n^2 variables a_ik is 'eigentlich' (properly discontinuous). In modern terms it is the integer linear substitution vec(a) -> (U^T ⊗ I_n) vec(a), and U -> U^T ⊗ I is injective. The reason given is that for A ≠ 0 no U ≠ I has a fixed point. If aU = a, then column by column a u_j = a e_j. The first column gives the n equations sum_k a_ik x_k = a_i1, the second gives sum_k a_ik y_k = a_i2, and so on. Since det a ≠ 0 these have the unique solutions x = e_1, y = e_2, ..., so U = I.

The next page completes the argument. Perturbing a_ik -> a_ik + b_ik with |b_ik| < eps (keeping A ≠ 0) yields only finitely many integer solution systems, so eps can be taken small enough that there are none. In footnote form: the function sum |a u_j - a e_j| has a positive minimum over integer U ≠ I. This gives disjointness of small images. One then grows the cube until contact, separates by supporting hyperplanes, and iterates to tile the space, giving the 'Urbereich'. Planned applications are automorphic functions of n^2 complex variables and higher continued-fraction algorithms.
errors: The fixed-point-freeness of the action on {A≠0} alone does not imply proper discontinuity. One also needs discreteness of the integer matrices, i.e. that only finitely many integer U map a compact neighbourhood into itself. Hilbert supplies this on the next page via the finiteness/perturbation argument, so on this page the 'denn' is incomplete rather than wrong.

The claim that the reduced domain in the n^2-dimensional space of linear forms is bounded by finitely many hyperplanes is stated without proof and is delicate. Minkowski-type reduction conditions on a matrix a are quadratic in the a_ik (they involve |a u|^2), so they are linear only in the coefficient space of the quadratic form a^T a (dimension n(n+1)/2). The linearity must come either from Hilbert's specific cube (sup-norm) construction or from a different parametrisation. As stated it is unjustified.

The question 'Inhalt for A=1' is ambiguous. det = 1 is a hypersurface of dimension n^2-1, so one must mean either the induced measure or the cone volume {|det| <= 1}. This is not a mathematical error.

results.what: Reduced domain of n linear forms (GL_n(Z) acting on R^{n^2} by a -> aU) is a convex region bounded by finitely many hyperplanes, whose images accumulate only at det = 0.
results.modern_name: Finiteness/convex polyhedrality of a fundamental domain for GL_n(Z) (Minkowski reduction domain; Siegel sets)
results.usually_credited_to: Hermite (1850s), Minkowski (Diskontinuitätsbereich für arithmetische Äquivalenz, 1905; earlier announcements around 1891)

results.what: Question whether the volume of the reduced domain with A=1 is finite and what its value is (attributed to Minkowski).
results.modern_name: Minkowski–Siegel volume formula: Lebesgue volume of {a in fundamental domain : |det a| <= 1} = zeta(2)zeta(3)...zeta(n)/n

results.what: Construction of a fundamental domain by growing a cube around a point and all its GL_n(Z)-images until contact, separating by supporting hyperplanes and iterating.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet/Voronoi-type (Ford/Dirichlet domain) construction of a fundamental polyhedron for a properly discontinuous group
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1850), Poincaré and Klein (1880s) for Fuchsian groups; Voronoi (1908) for lattices

results.what: The integral action on x is improperly discontinuous, while the induced holoedrically isomorphic action on the n^2 coefficients is free on {det ≠ 0}, by unique solvability of a u_j = a e_j.
results.modern_name: Free (and proper) right action of a discrete subgroup GL_n(Z) on GL_n(R)

deep.surprise_reason: These are research-plan notes on Minkowski's reduction theory. They record Minkowski's then-open volume question and sketch a Dirichlet-style construction of a fundamental domain for GL_n(Z) in n^2 dimensions, with the aim of building automorphic functions of n^2 variables. The Hilbert–Minkowski exchange on this topic is well known, and the results themselves are standard and credited to Minkowski and Siegel. The specific geometric 'growing cube' plan is a mildly notable unpublished detail, not a new result.

checkable.asserts: For det(a) ≠ 0 the system sum_k a_ik x_k = a_i1 has the unique solution x = e_1 (no nontrivial fixed point).
Second column system gives y = e_2, hence aU = a forces U = I.
The induced substitution on the n^2 variables, vec(a) -> (U^T ⊗ I) vec(a), is integral with determinant det(U)^n = ±1.
